# 039 · Protected access without the receiver rule opens every superclass object to a subclass

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 1 of 120 cases changed** | security, functional | critical | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`AccessControl#check`](../../../examples/demo/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/link/AccessControl.java) | [B8: Behavioural contracts](../../../lib/README.md) |

> Access control at resolution time admits a `protected` member from a subclass in another package only through an object of the subclass itself, as JVMS §5.4.4 requires in its "furthermore" clause. A developer drops the clause: a subclass inherits its superclass's protected members, and the receiver's type is the type checker's business. The behavioural contract of the check, 120 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in one: a protected instance member on an arbitrary object of the superclass is now accessible from a subclass in another package.

## The change

For a `protected` member and a subclass in another package, answer `true` instead of `staticMember || objectrefIsCurrentOrSubclass`. The receiver check duplicates one the type checker performs (§4.10.1.8), and resolution should decide on the classes alone. The tests for public, private, package and protected access, including a subclass elsewhere on its own objects and on a static member, all pass.

**Before** ([`AccessControl.java`](../../../examples/demo/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/link/AccessControl.java), line 25):

```java
    case PACKAGE_PRIVATE -> relation == Relation.SAME_CLASS || relation == Relation.SAME_NEST || relation == Relation.SAME_PACKAGE;
    case PROTECTED -> switch (relation) {
        case SAME_CLASS, SAME_NEST, SAME_PACKAGE -> true;
        // A subclass elsewhere reaches a protected instance member only through its own objects: the
        // objectref must be of D or a subclass of D, not just any C.
        case SUBCLASS_IN_OTHER_PACKAGE -> staticMember || objectrefIsCurrentOrSubclass;
        case UNRELATED -> false;
    };
};
```

**After:**

```java
    case PACKAGE_PRIVATE -> relation == Relation.SAME_CLASS || relation == Relation.SAME_NEST || relation == Relation.SAME_PACKAGE;
    case PROTECTED -> switch (relation) {
        case SAME_CLASS, SAME_NEST, SAME_PACKAGE -> true;
        // A subclass inherits the protected members of its superclass; the receiver's type is the
        // type checker's business (it is part of verification, not of resolution).
        case SUBCLASS_IN_OTHER_PACKAGE -> true;
        case UNRELATED -> false;
    };
};
```

```diff
--- a/examples/demo/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/link/AccessControl.java
+++ b/examples/demo/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/link/AccessControl.java
@@ -25,9 +25,9 @@ public final class AccessControl {
             case PACKAGE_PRIVATE -> relation == Relation.SAME_CLASS || relation == Relation.SAME_NEST || relation == Relation.SAME_PACKAGE;
             case PROTECTED -> switch (relation) {
                 case SAME_CLASS, SAME_NEST, SAME_PACKAGE -> true;
-                // A subclass elsewhere reaches a protected instance member only through its own objects: the
-                // objectref must be of D or a subclass of D, not just any C.
-                case SUBCLASS_IN_OTHER_PACKAGE -> staticMember || objectrefIsCurrentOrSubclass;
+                // A subclass inherits the protected members of its superclass; the receiver's type is the
+                // type checker's business (it is part of verification, not of resolution).
+                case SUBCLASS_IN_OTHER_PACKAGE -> true;
                 case UNRELATED -> false;
             };
         };
```

</details>

## What the verifier found

The behaviour changed for 1 of the 120 possible inputs. Each row is a concrete input that shows the difference:

| Input | The contract says | The code now does |
|---|---|---|
| `check(PROTECTED, SUBCLASS_IN_OTHER_PACKAGE, false, false)` | `false` | `true` |

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

The receiver rule is what makes `protected` mean "my subclasses, on their own instances" rather than "anyone who extends me, on anything". Without it, `class Attacker extends Base` in another package can read and write the protected fields and call the protected methods of every `Base` object it gets a reference to, which is why `Object.clone` and `Object.finalize` are protected and why the rule is in the JLS (§6.6.2.1) as well as the JVMS. The developer's premise is half right: the type checker does check the receiver, when it verifies the bytecode. Resolution is the only check for code the verifier did not see, for reflective access that goes through the same access control, and for the day the verifier is turned off; the two checks are deliberately redundant. The test for a subclass elsewhere covers the allowed case (its own object) and the static case; the forbidden case, an instance member on a foreign object, is the one case that changed.

## Why the verdict is right

The check is a pure function of four finite inputs: a visibility, a relation, and two booleans. The tool proves purity from the bytecode, runs all 120 inputs in its interpreter, and compares the outcomes with the committed contract. One differs: `check(PROTECTED, SUBCLASS_IN_OTHER_PACKAGE, false, false)`, the instance member on an object that is not of the referring class or a subclass of it, `false` before and `true` after. The other 119 cases, including the three the tests cover for the same visibility and relation, are unchanged, which is exactly why the tests pass.

## What to do

Revert, and keep the comment that points at §5.4.4's "furthermore" clause and at §4.10.1.8, so that the redundancy reads as intended rather than as duplication. The contract keeps all 120 cases under review; the one that changed here is the one to add a test for.

## Evidence

The proof trusted these JDK APIs to be pure: `java.lang.Enum.ordinal`, `java.lang.MatchException.<init>`, `java.lang.Record.<init>`, `java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch`, `java.util.List.copyOf`, `java.util.List.of`, `java.util.Objects.requireNonNull`.
